articles.title: Is this football's greatest superfan? 1,503 matches in a row and still counting...
articles.summary: The sudden hiatus imposed on football by the coronavirus outbreak hasn't yet endured quite long enough for QPR's very own 'superfan' Chris Kemp to be suffering withdrawal symptoms.
articles.body:
Right now, it feels like the close season, he says - but before long the R's fanatic will begin feeling the void of a prolonged period without football even more than most.

The 52-year-old civil servant has attended every one of his team's last 1,503 competitive matches - a run which stretches back more than 30 years to a 1-0 defeat against Manchester City at Maine Road in September 1989.

Of more immediate concern is the prospect of football restarting behind-closed-doors with Chris unable to attend, and therefore forced to break his incredible run, even if it won't be the first challenge it has faced.

"Do I legitimately remove those games from my run because they aren't games I can attend, and then resume as soon as football properly starts up again?" asks Chris.

"There have been a few other close shave incidents down the years which threatened the run.

"We had a blowout in the fast lane of the motorway once, which was an interesting experience. Fortunately, I wasn't the one driving.

"We played Southampton away at The Dell one season. We struggled with traffic and diversions. A friend of mine was driving slightly over the speed limit, shall we say, with a road atlas in one hand and the steering wheel in the other, trying to get us to the game.

"We eventually just dumped the car, found a police officer and ran to the ground after he'd given us directions. We ended up sitting down just as the teams came out.

"There was the problem of Luton's ban on away fans in the 1980s, too. A group of us managed to get into the main stand at Kenilworth Road and an enclave of QPR fans sang "You'll never ban a Rangers fan," so that fixture was always a concern logistically."

This week's EFL restart talks mean that bit more to Chris, who is awaiting confirmation from QPR's club historian that the games he has seen in his run cover more than 25 per cent of all the matches Rangers have played in their history since formation in 1882.

The 'man-cave' at this home in Wanstead, East London houses his collection of more than 50 QPR shirts, hundreds of matchday programmes, framed pictures, signed photos, his complete set of all 872 Roy of the Rovers comics and other weird and wonderful mementoes from his years of dedication to the Superhoops.

Chris, who works for the prison service, reckons he's spent around £80,000 on tickets and travel alone as he trekked all over England and Wales watching QPR.

"I really started supporting QPR at the end of the 1975/76 season when Wolves were playing Liverpool, who needed to lose for QPR to win the league title," explains Chris, who grew up in Harrow, a few miles from the Kiyan Prince Foundation Stadium.

"I liked the sound of the team name and I had a vague recollection that they played in London, so I thought I'd make QPR my team. The first game I went to was in 1977/78 when we were at home to Newcastle.

"My dad absolutely hated football. I was actually taken by my nan's decorator, who knew I was interested in football and was a season-ticket holder at QPR.

"He took me along and sat me on a wooden stool to I could see above the concrete wall and out on to the pitch.

"My 1,500th game was away at Nottingham Forest earlier in the season. My last game was Preston away. We hadn't won there in 40 years."

Chris has been plunged into some compromising situations by his slavish devotion to Rangers. It means he schedules his arrival for three hours before kick-off to allow for delays when driving to away games with friends.

In 1998, he planned the birth of his daughter Nicola with his ex-wife in the hope that his first-born would arrive in pre-season to avoid missing games.

"This was 1998 and I didn't have a mobile phone," he said.

"Instead, I had a pager and the understanding was that my wife at the time would message me and wherever I was, I'd just leave and come home.

"At the time, we were in the second tier and we were making four hour trips all over the country. Realistically, there wasn't a cat in hell's chance that I'd be leaving the game. I just hope my ex-wife isn't reading this.

"We were playing two games in a week in November 1998 against Barnsley on the Wednesday, then Bolton on the Saturday - both at Loftus Road.

"I remember patting the bump and saying 'don't pop out just yet because daddy's going to football - but I'll let you know when it's safe to do so'.

"I came back from the Barnsley game, which we won - and mentioned to the bump that if he or she fancied popping out now, then all well and good.

"Sure enough, my ex-wife's waters broke on the Thursday morning, and Nicola was delivered at 3.06pm that day. Then the following Saturday, Kevin Gallen gave us the lead against Bolton at 3.06pm - and I felt that was an omen."

Chris has won multiple Supporter of the Year awards and has been presented with a signed shirt by QPR whenever he reached a major milestone.

In the week leading up to his 1,500th against Forest in February, he received a personal message of congratulations from manager Mark Warburton. He has a programme from every one of those games, although most of them are still in his ex-wife's loft.

Among the landmarks was witnessing Liverpool's last league championship triumph when Kenny Dalglish's side beat QPR 2-1 at Anfield in April 1990 to seal their 18th title.

Chris also saw Manchester City lift the Premier League with that dramatic Sergio Aguero winner against QPR in added-time at the Etihad eight years ago.

Understandably, it's the famous results by his own team that stand out most for Chris.

"The 2014 Play-Off final at Wembley as it was the first time I'd seen us win there," he said. "After having a player sent off, I didn't think we'd be in with a shout of winning, so to do it in the last minute was just amazing.

"There were other games like our first win at Anfield in 1991 and then nine months later beating Manchester United 4-1 at Old Trafford on New Year's Day 1992.

"We also won for the first time at Manchester City and Nottingham Forest during the run.

"There was a game at Port Vale in 1997 when we were 4-0 down, which should have been five as they had a goal wrongly chalked off. We came back to draw 4-4.

"A couple of years later we were 3-0 down at Stockport in midweek and fought back to draw 3-3 in the second half. Chris Kiwomya put an effort just past the post in the last minute, which would have completed the turnaround.

"I regret the fact that none of this run has been in Europe. That's a real shame as I would like to have at least tested my ability to reach foreign shores. I'm not sure Cardiff, Wrexham and Swansea really count!"

QPR's last game at promotion-chasing Preston on March 7 saw them record their standout result of the season when they won at Deepdale for the first time since 1980, coming from a goal down to win 3-1 with ten men.

It set Rangers up for what many at the club felt would be a late push for the Championship Play-Offs and a possible return to the top flight after a five-year absence.

Chris is an elite runner who has completed four London marathons - he was among many QPR fans who felt their team was hitting their stride at just the right time before coronavirus signalled the abrupt halt.

Chris has adapted his life without QPR for the time-being - so how exactly has he done it?

"My brain is telling me the hiatus hasn't gone on long enough for it to be a problem," he said.

"So I'm trying to keep my routine as regular as possible. I still wear a QPR shirt on a Saturday morning and I do my normal ParkRun which I'd usually do early on the morning of a home game.

"I've regressed back a bit towards my childhood and started reading old copies of my Roy of the Rovers magazines.

"QPR's official website have also been doing this amazing feature called 'Rangers Rewind,' where they're showing historic games or ones from earlier in the season.

"I still have a bite to eat before I do all that. Even after the games have finished, I spend a bit of time in the man cave."

And the one QPR-related thing Chris hasn't done in a while?

That'll be watching the R's live on TV - which he hasn't done since 1986.

articles.title: Mikel Arteta, Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola started their paths to the top at Antiguoko: 'If I really think about it, it's absolutely crazy'
articles.summary: Born within 15 miles of each other and only seven months apart, the managers of Arsenal, Chelsea and Liverpool are all products of Antiguoko; Sky Sports visited the tiny Basque club to hear how it all began for Mikel Arteta, Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola
articles.body:
"The centre circle was just over there," says Roberto Montiel, the club's long-serving coach and vice-president, as he takes a seat in what is now a public park. He rubs his thumb and forefinger together as he recalls the texture of the old playing surface.

"The pitch wasn't like the new one up there. It was smaller and made of small stones, like gravel. The balls weren't like the ones now either. When they got wet, they became heavy. You would slip and slide, and if you fell, you'd end up with a terrible scrape."

The games played here by this neighbourhood club's celebrated alumni, two of whom meet as managers when Arsenal face Chelsea on Sky Sports on Sunday, are the stuff of local legend.

"Even then you could see their vision for the game," adds Montiel.

"On this pitch made of gravel, trying to pass those balls when it was raining, with puddles all over the place, with everything getting dirty. Honestly, it was something special to watch. The teams from those '81 and '82 generations were incredible."

Arteta and Iraola played in the latter age group; Alonso the former. "It was like a national team of the best players in the area and it made us an unbeatable team," says Alvaro Parra, a former Antiguoko team-mate and close friend of Arteta's.

"I remember games against Real Sociedad that were so easy. They would come to play us and we would beat them 5-0. Athletic Club would come and we would beat them as well. We won all the leagues. The team became known as the Basque Dream Team."

The club continues to turn out talent. Over at their offices, a mile further into town, near Ondarreta beach, Montiel jokes that they need more wall space to continue displaying signed shirts from a list of top-division graduates that now runs to more than 40 names.

Those of Arteta, Alonso and Iraola hold pride of place.

Their former colleagues are used to their success. But it remains a source of wonder, even to them, that these three Antiguoko players, born within 15 miles of each other, only seven months apart, in Gipuzkoa, the smallest province in Spain, have come this far.

"If I really think about it, it's absolutely crazy that our three friends are managing these Premier League teams," says Parra. "Sometimes I turn on the TV and say, 'Oh, it's Mikel! Oh, it's Xabi! What's happened here?'" adds Mikel Yanguas, another old team-mate.

Arteta: 'He was like a predator on the pitch'

Arteta was the pick of them growing up. "He had something different," says Yanguas, who played as a striker. "He was small but very technical and very clever. He played right behind me and he was always thinking about his next pass. I just needed to run."

Yanguas, who later moved to Barcelona's La Masia academy with Arteta, jokes that his old team-mate made him look better than he was. Parra, a former centre-back, feels similarly. "I just had to pass the ball to Mikel Arteta. Mikel Arteta to Yanguas. Goal."

Montiel is full of stories, many of them set on the old gravel pitch, and many of which highlight Arteta's intelligence, even as a boy. "The one I like to tell, and the one that stays with me most, shows that he was a player who was so alert to everything," he says.

"It was right over there, in midfield. The referee blew for a drop ball, and just as he let it bounce, Arteta flicked it away with the outside of his boot and hit a long pass across the pitch for a team-mate who was on his own to score - and that was against Real Sociedad."

There was an edge to Arteta too - even when playing up a year with Alonso. "He had a real competitive look about him," adds Montiel.

"He was super-attentive to everything you said. He showed an interest in everything. And then, when he went on the pitch, he was a predator. And that was against players a year older. I don't even need to tell you what he was like against players of his own age."

Arteta's competitiveness is one of his defining qualities as a manager. It was evident off the pitch as well as on it growing up.

Montiel remembers Arteta sliding, Jurgen Klinsmann-style, down the hallway of his house in Liverpool after beating him at PlayStation during a visit while he was at Everton.

"Whatever game you played with him, you would always lose," adds Parra. "If you played PlayStation, you would lose. If you played ping pong, you would lose. He was very, very competitive. If you beat him at anything, he would get angry and go home."

Parra chuckles as he utters the last line. He and Arteta were otherwise inseparable, their friendship, and holidays together, continuing even after his career took him abroad.

"After the year he made his debut with Paris Saint-Germain, he called me and said, 'Alvaro, pack your suitcase, we're going to Marbella.'" Parra has no photographs of that trip, lamentably. But he reaches for his phone and flicks through a selection of others.

Parra cherishes the memories. But Arteta, he stresses, was also organised and disciplined, in all aspects of his life, including his studies. "His parents instilled that in him."

Those qualities helped when he made the move to Barcelona aged only 15. Yanguas, although similarly talented according to those who first spotted him playing on La Concha beach with Arteta, never settled and returned home the following year.

"Mikel had a better capacity to adapt," he says. "He was quickly speaking to the other people at La Masia. I think he demonstrated that in other countries too, in France, in Scotland, in England. He always had the ability to adapt to any environment."

Iraola: 'A great team-mate and quiet leader'

Back in Berio, we have moved up the slope from the site of Antiguoko's old pitch to their new one, where an U16s team are being put through their paces under the midday sun.

"This is a very good group," says Montiel, before gesturing towards a slight figure in central midfield who stands out for his technical quality. "He had an offer from Real Sociedad but preferred to stay with us," he adds, with more than a hint of pride.

Real Sociedad and Athletic are signing Antiguoko players at ever-younger ages, Montiel says. But for some, the education on offer at Antiguoko is reason to stay. The coach overseeing this session, Iñigo Iraola, cousin of Andoni, is certainly from good footballing stock.

Like the older Iraola, who returned to Antiguoko as a coach while studying for his badges following his playing career, Iñigo came through the club's youth ranks as a player.

"The first game I ever watched was here in Berio, when Andoni came back with Athletic Club as an U18," he says. "From then on I always saw him as a role model and an example to follow."

He remembers Andoni taking him to buy his first pair of football boots. "They were Adidas boots," he says, smiling. "I went to buy them with him on my birthday here in San Sebastian. He was already playing for Athletic, so it was special for me to go with him."

Iraola is remembered differently to Arteta as a boy at Antiguoko.

"Mikel was captain of the team, he took responsibility," says Parra. "Andoni was more introverted, but at the same time he had incredible ability, and even if he was quieter, he was always a fun and polite guy, a great team-mate, and popular in the group."

"He was one of my favourites," adds Montiel. "Playing out wide, he didn't get as many touches as those in the centre, but every time he got to the byline, he would beat two or three players, make a pass and we'd score. He could work wonders with the ball."

He had the same competitive streak as Arteta. And although he was more reserved, as Parra explains, he had his moments.

"In our team, he played as a right winger and had a really important role," says Parra. "But when he went to Athletic, their manager Ernesto Valverde moved him to full-back.

"At first, he didn't like it at all. He even got angry, asking, 'Why are you putting me in defence?' But Valverde knew he was going to be an incredible full-back because he had the quality and the ability to take on players and get all the way up the pitch."

Iraola's leadership abilities emerged later, first as captain of Athletic, where he ended up making 510 appearances, then as a manager.

"One thing I really admire about Andoni is the kind of leader he is," says his cousin. "He isn't going to raise his voice above everyone else. He's a quieter, understated kind of leader who has more of an impact through the example he sets his players every day."

Ignacio Azpilicueta likes to joke that he had the best view in football.

As the central defender who occupied the space directly behind Alonso at Antiguoko, he enjoyed a front-row seat as his teenaged team-mate began to find his passing range.

"He played as the midfield pivot right in front of me, so I had the privilege of seeing Xabi's best passes from my position, right at the point when he developed the physical power and ball-striking ability that he went on to show for so many years."

Alonso had always been a good player. "He won the ball back a lot, played with two feet, and all of his passes were good," says Montiel. Azpilicueta recalls friends commenting on Alonso's ability during intra-school tournaments on La Concha beach.

He would come alive on the pitch. "He was really passionate," says Yanguas. "He really lived the game." But starting out at Antiguoko, few felt stardom beckoned for him.

"I remember our first sessions together and I would say I don't remember feeling that he was going to become the football star he is today," says Azpilicueta, who is no relation to the former Chelsea defender of the same name but had a good career of his own.

"He had a good touch, but physically he wasn't by any means the biggest or the strongest or the quickest. It took him a while to grow."

His trajectory, both physically and in terms of his career, changed in his U17 year. "I would say that was the moment when he really took off," says Azpilicueta. "He'd always had that intelligence, but now it was accompanied by that physical development."

"At that age, you could see he was going to be a first division player," says Parra. "Maybe not that he was going to win the Champions League, but you could see was going to be a top-level player."

According to Azpilicueta, he also benefitted from the qualities of humility and intelligence evident in Arteta and Iraola.

"I would say he was a very normal kid, like the rest of us. He didn't stand out in any particular way. He had a sense of humour. He was a good friend to his friends. But above all, he was very intelligent. He always made good decisions, on and off the pitch.

"I would say that has been a big part of his success."

So how does this little club do it? Arteta, Alonso and Iraola are of course their best-known graduates but more recent ones include Arsenal's Martin Zubimendi, their second World Cup winner after Alonso, and Rayo Vallecano boss Iñigo Perez.

Some point to the club's scouting in the area - "Oscar Landa, our sporting director, has a 95 per cent success rate," says Montiel - others to the atmosphere created by the longevity and commitment of their staff. But it usually comes back to the same thing.

"We've never changed the DNA of Antiguoko," says Montiel. "Competitive instinct, intensity and sporting discipline are non-negotiable." It is surely no coincidence that his old mentee Arteta uses that same term in reference to his managerial philosophy.

"We try to instil the values of sacrifice, discipline, hard work, teamwork and competitiveness," adds Iñigo Iraola. "I think it also reflects what the Basque player is: dedicated and committed to working hard every day. I think that's what makes us special."

Arteta, Alonso and Iraola personify those traits, as much managers as they did as players.

"The results should be seen in sporting terms, but also in human terms," says the club's general director Gorka Azpeita. "Beyond the footballing talent they have, it's important to highlight what they're like as people. They should be seen for the values they have, the people they are, and how it's enabled them to get where they are."

The only remaining question, then, is who they will be rooting for when Arteta and Alonso go head to head some 600 miles away in north London on Sunday. "That's like choosing between Mum and Dad," says Azpeita, laughing. "A draw would be perfect."

Watch Arsenal vs Chelsea live on Sky Sports Premier League and Main Event from 4pm on Sunday; kick-off 4.30pm

'The club that conquered the Premier League' is available to watch on YouTube and will be shown on Super Sunday ahead of the game

articles.title: Latest Heisman Trophy 2026 Odds as Arch Manning, Jeremiah Smith Rise
articles.summary: A few of the Heisman Trophy's greatest contenders took centerstage on Saturday, and they acquitted themselves well in the race's very early stages.
articles.body:
A few of the Heisman Trophy's greatest contenders took centerstage on Saturday, and they acquitted themselves well in the race's very early stages.

Here's a look at the latest odds for the top 10 contenders following the 3:30 p.m. ET set of games via FanDuel Sportsbook .

Five of those 10 players took the field Saturday. Here's how they did.

Texas quarterback Arch Manning began his second season as the Longhorns' starter by completing 20-of-27 passes for 305 yards, four touchdowns and one interception in a 59-7 home win over Texas State. Two of the TD passes went to Cam Coleman (six and 20 yards).

Manning's day was done with 7:55 left in the third quarter after he found Hollywood Smothers for a 13-yard touchdown pass to put Texas up 41-7.

He and the No. 5 Longhorns have a tougher test next week when the Longhorns host the No. 1 Ohio State Buckeyes in a rematch of last year's season opener, when OSU won 14-7. However, a strong showing from Manning could absolutely vault him into the early Heisman lead.

Speaking of the Buckeyes, Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith caught eight passes for 151 yards and two touchdowns in the first half alone to lead the No. 1 Buckeyes to a 56-3 home win over Ball State to begin the season.

Smith was sensational, making a 48-yard touchdown catch in air-tight coverage to open the scoring.

He also got a nifty toe-tap touchdown in the final seconds of the second quarter to put OSU up 27-3.

Since 2000, 21 quarterbacks have won the Heisman compared to just three running backs, one wide receiver and one two-way player. However, Smith is making a great case that he deserves the Heisman.

OSU quarterback Julian Sayin, of course, connected with Smith on those touchdowns. Sayin was about as good as one can get, completing 21-of-25 passes for 320 yards and three touchdowns (no picks).

His day was done early in the third quarter after his 13-yard pass to Bo Jackson set up the running back's 65-yard TD rush.

Oregon quarterback Dante Moore had a great day, completing 28-of-37 passes for 378 yards and three touchdowns in a 34-27 home win over the Boise State Broncos.

The No. 2 Ducks survived a serious upset attempt, though, as BSU was up 17-7 early.

However, Oregon scored 17 straight points for a 24-17 lead and later took a 34-27 advantage after Dante Moore and wide receiver Dakorien Moore, who showcased a tremendous effort, connected on a 62-yard touchdown.

Lastly, Indiana quarterback Josh Hoover had big cleats to fill after Heisman Trophy winner and national champion Fernando Mendoza left for the NFL, but he got off to a fantastic start, connecting on 13-of-16 passes for 231 yards and four touchdowns in a 52-16 home win over North Texas.

Hoover got busted up during the game after drawing a face mask penalty, but that didn't stop him from playing.

Ultimately, one of every four of Hoover's throws resulted in a touchdown pass.

Hoover and the Hoosiers will now face Howard on Saturday at noon ET.

articles.title: Jayden Daniels Excluded from LSU Video Highlighting Former Tigers in NFL After No. 5 Jersey Dispute
articles.summary: Washington Commanders quarterback and former LSU standout Jayden Daniels wasn't included in the Tigers' video highlighting the school's NFL players ahead of a matchup with Clemson on Saturday.
articles.body:
Washington Commanders quarterback and former LSU standout Jayden Daniels wasn't included in the Tigers' video highlighting the school's NFL players ahead of a matchup with Clemson on Saturday.

LSU alumni in the NFL who were featured in the video included Joe Burrow, Justin Jefferson, Ja'Marr Chase, Malik Nabers, Will Campbell, Patrick Queen, Mansoor Delane and Garrett Nussmeier.

Daniels, who wore No. 5 at LSU, previously sent the school a cease-and-desist letter that stemmed from the decision to allow cornerback D.J. Pickett to wear the same number on his jersey this season.

Daniels only played two seasons at LSU from 2022-23, but earned Heisman Trophy honors during his second year with the team.

articles.title: Go for it or not? Dave Aranda's 2-point decision that led to Baylor's loss to Auburn won't lose him his job, but he's running out of time regardless
articles.summary: You'd be hard-pressed to find anyone at Baylor who disagreed with Aranda's decision to go for two and a victory over Auburn. But not getting it still carries...
articles.body:
ATLANTA — Whenever Baylor has to make the ultimate call on Dave Aranda, it is unlikely to be clear-cut. He is too competent to crater and too well-liked to author his own demise, working at a school that would prefer not to buy out a football coach unless it has to.

But it is not a secret, least of all to Aranda, that his seventh season will be defined by decisions: The little ones he makes every week, followed by the big one his employer must render.

After the first of 12 data points is now in the rear-view mirror, it's imperative to start thinking about the question that can bring some of these fine margins into leader focus: How much credit does a coach get for doing the right thing but getting the wrong result?

Though perhaps not every fan would agree, you'd be hard-pressed to find anyone within the Baylor program who disagreed with Aranda's decision to go for two and a victory over Auburn on Saturday night after his quarterback, DJ Lagway, fought through an ankle sprain and threw a touchdown pass with nine seconds remaining.

Analytically, it was the right call. Emotionally, it was a risk worth taking. Practically, it was a no-brainer.

"There was no hesitation," Aranda said. "The book said to go for it, but it wasn't so much that. We had so many guys that were just doing everything they can to try to push through and close the game out. I just didn't feel playing longer was going to benefit us.

In the end, no matter how the season turns out, there will always be a what-if attached to Auburn 17, Baylor 16 . The 2-point play that offensive coordinator Jake Spavital drew up worked. Lagway made the throw, tight end Matthew Klopfenstein caught the ball and had what seemed to be a path to the end zone.

He just couldn't get there before Auburn safety Eric Winters wrapped him in a textbook tackle, getting him on the ground a mere inches from the goal line.

"I thought he was in," Aranda said. "You hear the call, you know what the play is, you're watching for it and you see it. I'm thinking it's points. For it not to be just sucks."

Five years ago, Aranda was on the opposite side of a similar play in a much more significant moment. In the 2021 Big 12 championship game, with just seconds to play, Oklahoma State had a fourth-down play at the 1-yard line to win the game. Running back Dezmon Jackson had what seemed to be a sure touchdown running for the corner of the end zone but felt the pressure from behind, reached for the pylon and came up tantalizingly short.

At that moment, Aranda's career seemed like a rocket ship. In his second year as a head coach, he had won a conference title, followed by beating Ole Miss in the Sugar Bowl. If anything, Baylor would've been concerned that he might end up getting lured back to a place like LSU, where he won a national title as defensive coordinator.

But since then, Aranda has posted three losing seasons in four years. Some of the issues were of his own making. Others, like Baylor ranking in the lower-tier of NIL spending in the Big 12, have been institutional obstacles.

The bottom line, though, is Baylor's attendance has cratered and there have not been enough quality wins to secure his future. Last November, in the midst of losing five out of six to end the season and athletic director Mack Rhoades resigning due to personal issues, Baylor announced that Aranda would return so that a new athletic director could come in and assess the football program.

That new athletic director is Doug McNamee, who previously worked at Baylor and left to work for Magnolia, the company founded by Chip and Joanna Gaines, who are among the school's biggest benefactors.

From now until the end of the season, taking the temperature of Baylor's key stakeholders is the reality McNamee will live every day. It's hard to imagine that a game like Saturday makes the picture any clearer.

Yes, Baylor fought hard, had an outstanding defensive game plan to bottle up Auburn's offense and made one clutch play after another on the 75-yard drive that gave the Bears a chance to win it with a 2-point conversion. To go for it in that moment, knowing the stakes, knowing the fragility of his tenure, is the kind of coaching that shows the courage of his convictions.

"We had nothing in our mind but next play," said receiver Gavin Freeman, who caught a touchdown on fourth-and-goal from the 5-yard line. "No matter what happens, just keep going. I have faith in my guys and we all had faith going forward because that's what we do in practice. That's what we practice all the time is winning the game."

But is that enough when it doesn't work?

As much as you can commend Aranda for almost getting off to an ideal start in a make-or-break year, this was not a game Baylor should not have lost.

When you have 436 offensive yards, you should score more than 16 points. When your defense forces three turnovers, you should capitalize. When you leave points on the board by missing a 42-yard field goal, then calling an ill-fated fourth down play in the third quarter instead of a 33-yard field goal in a game you lost by a single point, can you really say the head coach had a good day?

"Mistakes. That's why we lost," Aranda said. "That's what I told the team. Early in the game there's too many opportunities we had to finish drives, to put points on the board, and we didn't do it. I take the credit for that. I should have done a better job of coaching that. More games are lost than won, especially early in the season, and I could've communicated that better because I think we contributed to that tonight."

As always, Aranda was forthright, cerebral and emotionally even-keeled. It's part of what makes him hard to get your arms around. He is not a natural salesman, and Baylor's fan base has largely registered its vote on him last year with all the empty seats in McLane Stadium.

articles.title: Bryce Underwood, No. 16 Michigan Avoid WMU Upset Bid on Hail Mary, Big Ten Issues Statement on Clock
articles.summary: Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood uncorked a 47-yard Hail Mary pass that landed in wide receiver JJ Buchanan's hands for a game-winning touchdown with no time remaining as the No. 16 Wolverines survived a tremendous upset attempt from the visiting Western Michigan Broncos and won 13-12.
articles.body:
Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood uncorked a 47-yard Hail Mary pass that landed in wide receiver JJ Buchanan's hands for a game-winning touchdown with no time remaining as the No. 16 Wolverines survived a tremendous upset attempt from the visiting Western Michigan Broncos and won 13-12.

However, Michigan got that chance because officials deemed there was one second remaining on the clock after Underwood's previous Hail Mary attempt fell incomplete. Initially, the clock ran out and showed zero, but one second was put back after an official review.

The Big Ten issued a statement on the matter, and the Mid-American Conference did as well.

Michigan was a monstrous 27.5-point favorite heading into this game, per FanDuel Sportsbook . However, the Wolverines' offense couldn't get anything going between the touchdown-scoring opening drive and the final play. That didn't matter, though, as the Wolverines ultimately came through with the big win.

This game won't be without controversy, however. On the penultimate play , Underwood threw a Hail Mary that went through the end zone and into a throng of players that was navigating out of bounds.

Upon further review, the game clock hit zero before the pass was deflected off any players, meaning the contest should have ended.

Sports journalist and writer Rodger Sherman of the Sports! newsletter slowed down and edited the video of the play , and the ball is just a few feet away from coming in contact with anyone on the field when the clock shows zeroes.

It initially appeared that Western Michigan won the game, and the Broncos began celebrating. After an official review, however, referees put one second back on the clock. That led to Underwood's Hail Mary miracle and Michigan's great escape.

NBC rules analyst Terry McAulay questioned how Big Ten officials arrived at the conclusion that there was one second left on the clock.

Ultimately, the Big Ten has stated that Western Michigan safety Micah Davis was out of bounds when he touched the ball, which stops the clock and results in an incomplete pass ruling. The clock the Big Ten showed had one second left, although it clearly was not in sync with the NBC broadcast clock, which showed no time remaining.

People will be talking about the final second of the game for years, but there were (officially) 59 minutes and 59 seconds of game action before then as well.

Michigan's offense looked crisp to start thanks to an 11-play, 75-yard drive capped by Underwood's one-yard touchdown leap on 4th-and-goal.

However, Michigan's offense went completely stagnant from there thanks in large part to a great WMU defensive effort. The Wolverines' next four drives went a combined 26 yards and ended in punts.

Michigan's last first half drive was calamitous. The Wolverines had the ball on their own 27-yard line with nine seconds left and little chance to score but decided to throw the ball. WMU linebacker Dillon Moore came up with a pick, and Kelly hit a 45-yard field goal with no time left.

Both teams traded punts to start the third quarter, but Western Michigan then engineered a 20-play, 71-yard drive that took nearly an entire quarter's worth of time (13:40 to be exact) off the clock. Kelly's 39-yard field goal gave WMU a 9-7 lead with 10:25 left.

Both teams traded punts again, but WMU was winning the field position battle and pinned Michigan on its own seven-yard line with 3:04 remaining.

Three plays later, Underwood ran for 13 yards to the Michigan 31, but WMU defensive back Joshua Franklin forced a fumble, recovered by teammate KJ Burley.

The Broncos had a chance to run the clock out on their next drive and had a 3rd-and-2 on the Michigan 12-yard line, but a fumbled snap (which they recovered) led to a two-yard loss. Kelly hit his fourth field goal, this time from 33 yards out.

Michigan's final drive started with two incomplete passes, but Underwood found Buchanan for a 28-yard strike on 3rd-and-10. He then spiked the ball, leading to the final two plays.

This game served as Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham's debut with the team. Whittingham, who was Utah's head coach from 2005-2025 before arriving in Ann Arbor, couldn't have scripted a more dramatic start.

He spoke after the game about the emotion of the moment, the issues Michigan encountered during the matchup and the infamous second left on the clock.

WMU head coach Lance Taylor took the high road when asked about what happened at the end of the game.

The biggest question, of course, is what the officials saw leading to there being one second left.

As of late Saturday night into early Sunday morning, there was no word, although reporters requested a pool report (i.e. a designated media member speaks with a game official regarding a matter).

It appears, though, that officials won't be speaking on the matter.

One can guess that the ending to this game will be much-discussed in the ensuing days. It'll certainly go down in history.

Michigan Stadium isn't immune to Hail Mary passes. In 1979, Michigan wideout Anthony Carter hauled one in to beat Indiana, 27-21. In 1994, Colorado quarterback Kordell Stewart found wide receiver Michael Westbrook to beat Michigan, 27-26. It's not immune to major upsets either, as then Division I-FCS Appalachian State notably beat No. 5 Michigan 34-32 in 2007.

This time around, Michigan found itself on the right side of Hail Mary history while avoiding another historical upset.

Looking ahead, WMU and Michigan move along to Saturday's Week 2 contests.

The Wolverines will remain home next Saturday but will take on an extremely tough No. 10 Oklahoma squad, which opened the season with a 51-0 win over UTEP.

The Broncos will return home to host Monmouth.

We had several where the spot was questioned and reviewed and those calls went our way, the review went our way. So, listen, I'll let our commissioner and those guys handle it. articles.title: No. 16 Michigan beats Western Michigan 13-12 on controversial Hail Mary after clock was reset to 1 second
articles.summary: Michigan made the most of its extra play
articles.body:
No. 16 Michigan avoided an upset loss to Western Michigan on Saturday night with a lot of help from instant replay.

Bryce Underwood hit JJ Buchanan for an incredible 47-yard Hail Mary as time expired for a 13-12 win. The pass came after the ball was snapped with one second left after Underwood's previous Hail Mary appeared to fall incomplete with no time remaining.

After a short review, a second was added back to the clock. And then Buchanan made the catch.

NBC's numerous replays of the first Hail Mary showed that the ball was not close to touching a Western Michigan player who had stepped out of bounds when he jumped for the pass until the clock showed 0:00. Rules analyst and former referee Terry McAuley was unable to come up with a concrete explanation for why a second was added to the clock.

"The ball isn't even close to touching the player when it goes to zero," McAuley said after he told viewers that he was informed that the clock on the bottom left of the screen was the stadium clock and in sync with the replay. "Now their Hawk Eye system apparently either was — had a different sync or whatever and they came up with one second when it touched the players. I don't see how that happened assuming our clock is correct. It is clearly not touching the player. It is clearly still in the air when the clock goes to zero on our screen. So the Big Ten's going to have to tell a lot of us how did they get to one second on this play."

Here's how the first Hail Mary looked in real time.

The second-chance Hail Mary was Buchanan's second massive catch of the final drive. He was responsible for all 75 yards on the drive as he caught a 28-yard pass on third down to get Michigan across midfield and put the Wolverines in position to go for the end zone.

Michigan got the ball back for its final drive with 35 seconds to go after Western Michigan kicked a field goal to go up five points. The Broncos' fourth field goal of the game came after Underwood fumbled while trying to scramble for a first down with 1:40 to go.

That turnover was Michigan's third of the game and Underwood's second. He had a rough game and had just 95 passing yards before the final drive.

Western Michigan's offensive stats weren't pretty either, but they controlled the clock. The Broncos had just 221 total yards on 67 plays but held onto the ball for just over 40 minutes. WMU was 8-of-18 on third downs and had 16 first downs to Michigan's 12.

The Wolverines had 276 yards on 48 plays, but committed nine penalties and were just 3-of-10 on third downs.

Had the clock actually expired on the incomplete pass, the first game of coach Kyle Whittingham's tenure would have been an unmitigated disaster. The former Utah coach hired to clean up the mess left behind by the fired Sherrone Moore has a lot to go through when he watches film with his coaching staff.

Instead, Michigan is, somehow, 1-0, and the Big Ten will be doing a lot of explaining in the coming days to show just why the Wolverines deserve to have that win.

articles.title: Michigan's ruling explained: Analyst Terry McAulay presents only theory in which bizarre ending makes sense
articles.summary: Usually, a game is over when the clock hits zero.
articles.body:
The easy word for what happened at the end of No. 16 Michigan's win over Western Michigan is "controversial." That might not work, though, as everyone seems pretty unanimous on what happened.

With only a few seconds on the clock, Michigan attempted a 47-yard Hail Mary that fell incomplete as time seemingly expired. A replay review predictably ensued, with the Big Ten's replay center eventually deciding to put one second back on the clock.

Michigan's second Hail Mary attempt had a better outcome, with the Wolverines pulling off a wild 13-12 win .

However, anyone with the ability to pause and slo-mo the replay shown on television can tell you the clock clearly struck zero while the ball was in the air on the first attempt. The clock should have stopped as soon as Western Michigan safety Micah Davis touched the ball because he had stepped out of bounds. But, again, time expired while the ball was in the air.

There should not have been a final play, as far as any outside observer can tell. It is rare that a blown call feels this obvious, this blatantly irreconcilable with the plain fact of a clock on a screen.

It's not just a bad call, it's a call so bad it leaves us wondering how it's even possible.

There is, however, an explanation of what happened courtesy of NBC officiating analyst Terry McAulay. In the aftermath of the ruling, McAuley went through the replay with the broadcast booth and explained that while the NBC broadcast supposedly had the stadium clock synced up on its replay, the Big Ten's replay center might have had a different sync with its Hawk-Eye camera.

"The ball isn't even close to touching the player when it goes to zero. Now their Hawk-Eye system apparently either was — had a different sync or whatever and they came up with one second when it touched the players. I don't see how that happened, assuming our clock is correct. It is clearly not touching the player. The ball is clearly still in the air when the clock goes to zero on our screen. So the Big Ten's going to have to tell a lot of us how did they get to one second on this play."

That is all speculation, but it at least adds some sort of logic to an irrational sequence of events. It would still make the outcome an outrage, as a clock at the Big Ten replay center in Rosemont, Illinois, would be overruling the clock in Ann Arbor.

We do know one area where McAulay is 100% correct, though: The Big Ten has some explaining to do.

articles.title: Real Madrid suffer Marc Cucurella injury blow ahead of Inter Milan clash
articles.summary: After losing to Real Betis on Friday, Real Madrid are hoping to bounce back when they host Inter Milan in their Champions League opener on Tuesday. Jose Mour...
articles.body:
After losing to Real Betis on Friday , Real Madrid are hoping to bounce back when they host Inter Milan in their Champions League opener on Tuesday. Jose Mourinho failed to win European football's premier competition during his first spell in charge, and that failure will drive him to ensure that he achieves this goal second time around.

If they are to claim La Decimosexta come next June, Real Madrid must ensure they finish inside the top eight in the league phase, as this will see them avoid the jeopardy of the play-off round, which they have featured in on the two occasions since the new format premiered. Getting off to a good start against Inter will be crucial, although Mourinho looks set to be without one of his key players for the match.

In the closing stages of the Betis defeat, Marc Cucurella had to be replaced by Alvaro Carreras. Mourinho revealed in his post-match press conference that the full-back suffered with cramps, but it has since been reported that the 2026 World Cup winner is a major doubt to face the Nerazzurri because of this issue, as per MD .

Carreras poised for return to starting line-up

Cucurella will not be out for long, but the idea is that he does not recover in time to face Inter. Mourinho will know that taking any unnecessary risks with one of his key players would be unwise, which is why Carreras is likely to make his return to the starting line-up, having been left out for the matches against Malaga and Betis.

All being well, Real Madrid will be able to manage without Cucurella for the match against Inter. He should be fine to return for the encounter with Rayo Vallecano next weekend, at which point Los Blancos will try to return to winning ways on the domestic scene.

articles.title: 5 takeaways from Texas A&M’s season-opening shutout win
articles.summary: Going into the season, Texas A&M was viewed by some as a sleeper candidate to win the Southeastern Conference.  Likewise, returning quarterback Marcel Reed i...
articles.body:
Going into the season, Texas A&M was viewed by some as a sleeper candidate to win the Southeastern Conference.

Likewise, returning quarterback Marcel Reed is considered as a darkhorse Heisman Trophy contender.

If Saturday is any indication, Reed and the Aggies may very well cause some commotion in the SEC and national landscape. Reed completed 70% of his passes while throwing for 233 yards and two touchdowns as Texas A&M started its 2026 season with a 50-0 shutout win against Missouri State Saturday night at Kyle Field.

Here are some takeaways from the Aggies performance:

Reed ended his night completing 21-of-30 passes. His second completion resulted in the Aggies' opening TD, a 15-yard strike to Isaiah Horton that finished off A&M's first drive, which went 58 yards in eight plays.

Then late in the first half, Reed threw a strike over the middle to Mario Craver for a 12-yard score, giving A&M a 19-0 advantage.

"I think for the first game, I played well," Reed said postgame. "The team did pretty well. It was a slow start after the first touchdown. … (In the) second half, we bounced back and did what we were supposed to do.

"When you play in the first game of the season, you don't want to show all your stuff. We executed the base plays well enough (Saturday)."

One of A&M's - and Reed's concerns - entering the season was finding a comparable receiver to KC Concepcion, now with the Cleveland Browns.

The Aggies may have found a suitable replacement in Horton, like Concepcion a transfer, in this case coming over from Alabama, and Miami (Fla.) before that. In his Aggies' debut, Horton hauled in four passes for 76 yards.

"My first game as an Aggie was amazing," Horton said. "What I was told about the crowd, especially when we came out, I definitely felt it."

Also, in another bit of irony, Horton is wearing number 7 - which was Concepcion's jersey number last season.

"I thought it was cool that both of our #7 transfers scored the first touchdown of 2025 and 2026," Reed said. "Happy for Zay. I think he's going to be a great guy for us. You saw the vertical threat he can be. … Excited for what's in store for him and us."

While Horton is a newcomer to watch, along with Reed, there are other returning skill standouts at the Aggies' disposal. And they helped contribute to their opening-game showing.

Craver, another one of Reed's key targets, had the most receptions with five along with 41 yards and a TD. Versatile player Terry Bussey caught three passes and had a 10-yard TD run on the opening drive of the second half. Then, returning senior tailback Reuben Owens was the leading rusher with 77 yards on 17 carries.

The Aggies had more than 10 times the number of total yards than it had points. They finished with 505 yards on the night.

Seven different players had a carry, as the Aggies racked up 236 yards on the ground. And then A&M completed 25 passes, which went to 10 different receivers.

A&M was also 50% on third-down conversions (7-of-14) and a perfect 2-of-2 on fourth-down conversions. The Aggies also more than doubled their number of plays compared to the Bears, running 85 total plays to Missouri State's 40.

With Saturday's shutout, it was the first opening-game shutout for A&M since a 24-0 win against LSU in 1993.

A&M held Missouri State to just 67 total yards of offense. The Aggies also forced two turnovers, had one sack and six tackles for loss.

Noah Mikhail, a sophomore linebacker, was the top tackler with seven stops. The sack was recorded by defensive end Ryan Henderson, a San Diego State transfer who also had two TFLs and a forced fumble.

"Happy with how the defense came out and played," A&M coach Mike Elko said. "They played to the level we hoped that they would."

The Aggies also got a safety on special teams, when Missouri State muffed a punt, which squirted into the end zone and out, giving the Aggies a 9-0 lead late in the opening quarter. It was A&M's first safety since 2017.

A&M (1-0) is at home next Saturday to take on Arizona State. Kickoff from Kyle Field is set for 11 a.m.

articles.title: Lane Kiffin Wins LSU Debut vs. Dabo's Clemson by 41 Points, Box Score, Top Player Stats & Highlights
articles.summary: The Lane Kiffin-led LSU Tigers announced their presence with authority on the college football scene.
articles.body:
The Lane Kiffin-led LSU Tigers announced their presence with authority on the college football scene.

The 11th-ranked Tigers routed the Clemson Tigers 51-10 in Kiffin's first game in charge of the SEC program.

LSU scored 17 points in the first quarter, but the game didn't start well for the Bayou Bengals, as Sam Leavitt threw an interception on the second play from scrimmage.

Leavitt rebounded and led the Tigers on two scoring drives in the first quarter, the second of which resulted in a one-yard touchdown run from Dilin Jones.

LSU's defense got in on the party next with an interception return for a touchdown.

Leavitt and Co. took full control after that moment, as they went on to score 14 points in the second quarter and 13 points in the third.

Leavitt, an Arizona State transfer, ran for a pair of touchdowns to go along with his one scoring throw.

LSU will have one week out of the Saturday spotlight, as it plays the Louisiana Tech Bulldogs in Week 2.

Kiffin and Co. will be tested in back-to-back weeks to end September against top-10 teams. They face Kiffin's old team, the No. 9 Ole Miss Rebels, in Week 3 and the No. 8 Texas A&M Aggies in Week 4.

articles.title: B/R's 2026 College Football Experts Top 25 Rankings After Week 1
articles.summary: While Week 1 of the 2026 college football season didn't have a marquee upset, it wasn't without its fair share of excitement.
articles.body:
While Week 1 of the 2026 college football season didn't have a marquee upset, it wasn't without its fair share of excitement.

Oregon squeezed out a 34-27 victory over a Boise State squad that looked very much like the Group of Six headliner, Michigan was literally one second away from being upset by Western Michigan and Oregon State put a serious scare into Houston.

Beyond that, it was a lot of stat padding for the nation's elite against lesser competition, though LSU's lopsided win over Clemson carried a bit more cachet than most Week 1 victories.

Now it's time for Bleacher Report's first updated top 25 ranking of the new season, with the college football writing staff of David Kenyon, Adam Kramer, Joel Reuter and Brad Shepard making up our voting panel.

Editor's Note: These rankings will be updated after Week 1 games are completed on Sunday and Monday.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Arkansas-Pine Bluff (54-14) Next Week: at Kansas

Ousted by the breakout performance of Trinidad Chambliss at Ole Miss, Austin Simmons landed at Missouri in the transfer portal and showed out in his Tigers debut. He completed 17-of-19 passes for 252 yards and four touchdowns while helping build a 40-0 first-half lead before giving way to backup Matt Zollers, and the running game brought it home with 357 yards and four scores.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Oregon State (33-20) Next Week: vs. Southern

The Cougars were 20.5-point favorites in their opener, but led just 26-20 with 9:02 remaining in the fourth quarter following an Oregon State touchdown. They answered that score with an eight-play, 62-yard drive capped off by a Conner Weigman rushing touchdown to seal the victory, but it was a closer game than expected. Weigman finished with 305 passing yards, 30 rushing yards and two total touchdowns.

23. Kansas State (1-0, Previous Rank: 25)

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Nicholls (71-3) Next Week: vs. Washington State

With 312 rushing yards, six touchdowns and 7.1 yards per carry, the Wildcats running game simply overwhelmed FCS opponent Nicholls. Dual-threat quarterback Avery Johnson also got in on the fun, throwing for 199 yards and three touchdowns to go along with his 23 yards and one score on the ground. For those wondering, a 76-0 win over Ball State in 2000 still stands as the highest-scoring game in K-State history.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Northern Illinois (40-0) Next Week: vs. Iowa State

The Hawkeyes only managed to score 37 points against FCS opponent Albany in their season opener last year, so this was a banner start to the season offensively. A 289-7 edge in rushing yardage was the story of the game, with Kamari Moulton (11 carries, 183 yards, 2 TD) leading the Iowa charge. Seven penalties and a turnover give Iowa some things to clean up before their rivalry game against Iowa State.

Week 1 Result: at Ole Miss (Sunday) Next Week: vs. Villanova

Results and analysis will be added following the conclusion of Sunday's game.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Marshall (45-0) Next Week: at Temple

Despite throwing 64 touchdown passes over the last three seasons at Iowa State, Rocco Becht never had a four-touchdown game before Saturday, when he tallied 271 yards and four scores through the first drive of the second half before exiting with the outcome well in hand. The Nittany Lions defense surrendered 147 total yards, forced two turnovers and held the Thundering Herd to 1-of-11 on third down conversions.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Furman (56-9) Next Week: at Georgia Tech

The bad news: Tennessee's defense allowed 178 rushing yards and 4.9 yards per carry to a SoCon opponent. The good news: They countered with 329 rushing yards and 7.0 yards per carry on their end, and the defense ultimately limited the Paladins to nine points. True freshman quarterback Faizon Brandon also had a terrific debut, completing 13-of-17 pass attempts for 226 yards and three touchdowns while adding 68 yards and two more scores on the ground.

Week 1 Result: vs. Washington State (Sunday) Next Week: vs. Utah State

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Idaho (66-14) Next Week: vs. Arkansas

The Utes pounded out 364 rushing yards on 49 carries to grind an overmatched Idaho team into the ground, while quarterback Devon Dampier went 13-of-18 passing with 176 yards and three touchdowns before making his way to the sidelines following the opening drive of the second half. With a staggering 633-225 edge in total yardage, Utah was in complete control.

Week 1 Result: at Florida State (Monday) Next Week: vs. UC Davis

Results and analysis will be added following the conclusion of Monday's game.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Utah Tech (63-7) Next Week: vs. Arizona

The Cougars had seven different players record at least 20 rushing yards en route to a 308-yard, five-touchdown performance on the ground, and there was still enough meat left on the bone for Bear Bachmeier to tally 198 yards and three scores through the air. BYU built a 56-0 lead before Utah Tech put points on the board, and the Cougars defense forced four turnovers.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. East Carolina (48-10) Next Week: at Kentucky

A comical 227-2 advantage in rushing yardage was the story of the game for Alabama, as their defensive front proved to be an immovable object for the East Carolina running game. Keelon Russell tallied 249 passing yards, 86 rushing yards and a rushing touchdown in his first career start, showing early chemistry with Ryan Coleman-Williams, who had five catches for 130 yards. There is not another non-power conference opponent on the Crimson Tide's schedule until Chattanooga on Nov. 21.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Abilene Christian (33-10) Next Week: at Oregon State

The Red Raiders led 33-3 before allowing a touchdown late in the fourth quarter, and one of the nation's elite defenses last season looked the part once again, allowing 3.7 yards per pass and 2.6 yards per carry. The unit also tallied three sacks, six tackles for loss and seven pass deflections. Will Hammond completed 26-of-33 passes for 298 yards with a touchdown and an interception following an offseason of uncertainty amid the Brendan Sorsby saga.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Fresno State (39-0) Next Week: vs. Louisiana

The Trojans opened the year with a 42-26 victory over San Jose State that was not as close as the final score suggested, as USC's backup defenders allowed 23 fourth-quarter points. There was no late offensive surge on Friday night against Fresno State, as the Trojans pitched a shutout while allowing just 116 total yards and 1.3 yards per rush attempt. Jayden Maiava is 48-of-54 passing for 635 yards and five touchdowns during the 2-0 start.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Missouri State (50-0) Next Week: vs. Arizona State

A mere 67 yards and four first downs. That's all the Missouri State offense could muster against the Texas A&M defense in what might have been the most one-sided game in a Week 1 slate full of dominating performances. Meanwhile, the Aggies racked up 505 yards while owning the time of possession battle (43:03 to 16:57), with Marcel Reed throwing for 233 yards and two touchdowns.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. UTEP (51-0) Next Week: at Michigan

A Sooners defense expected to be among the best in the nation looked the part in Week 1, limiting UTEP to 198 total yards and a 2-of-13 showing on third-down conversions. Isaiah Sategna III had an 88-yard punt return touchdown and also caught one of three touchdown passes from John Mateer, who threw for 225 yards on only 11 completions.

Week 1 Result: vs. Louisville (Sunday) Next Week: vs. Charlotte

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Clemson (51-10) Next Week: vs. Louisiana Tech

Sam Leavitt lived up to the transfer portal hype in his LSU debut with 230 passing yards, 113 rushing yards and three total touchdowns, and LSU scored 51 unanswered points after allowing a first-quarter field goal. The bigger story was a lockdown performance by the Tigers defense, as Clemson went 0-for-12 on third-down conversions while recording just 74 total yards and punting 10 times before a garbage-time drive in the final minutes.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Boise State (34-27) Next Week: at Oklahoma State

There's a reason many are predicting Boise State to be the team that represents the Group of Six in the College Football Playoff field, and what was a close outcome could ultimately end up being a quality win for Oregon.

The Ducks trailed 17-14 at halftime and were locked in a 24-24 tie entering the fourth quarter. After the two teams traded field goals, Dakorien Moore made multiple defenders miss on a 62-yard touchdown reception from Dante Moore with 7:51 remaining that proved to be the game-winner.

Moore finished with 378 yards and three touchdowns through the air, and a 497-274 total yardage advantage showed that Oregon controlled the action offensively, even if it didn't lead to a comfortable victory.

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. North Texas (52-16) Next Week: vs. Howard

The defending champs probably allowed 16 more points than head coach Curt Cignetti would have liked, but it was nonetheless a dominant start to their title defense. Quarterback Josh Hoover hit fellow prized transfer Nick Marsh for a touchdown strike with his first pass attempt, on his way to a 231-yard, four-touchdown performance. North Texas actually outgained them 367-365 in total yardage, so the defense has some things to button up in the coming weeks.

5. Texas Longhorns (1-0, Previous Rank: 6)

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Texas State (59-7) Next Week: vs. Ohio State

Arch Manning threw for 305 yards and four touchdowns, though he was also picked off in the end zone for his first interception of the season, and he won't have the same margin of error in next week's matchup against Ohio State.

Defensively, the Longhorns did a great job slowing down North Texas quarterback Brad Jackson, limiting him to 177 total yards and zero touchdowns after he racked up 3,224 passing yards, 744 rushing yards and 38 total scores in 2025.

4. Georgia Bulldogs (1-0, Previous Rank: 5)

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Tennessee State (63-3) Next Week: vs. Western Kentucky

The Bulldogs found the end zone on each of their first five drives to build an early 35-0 lead, then parked quarterback Gunner Stockton and many other regulars on the sidelines amid a lopsided rout.

Stockton still finished with 202 passing yards and three touchdowns while completing 15 of 16 attempts, while running back Nate Frazier needed just four carries to tally 72 yards and three scores. All told, the Georgia offense piled up 660 total yards while only reaching third down six times.

Defensively, the Bulldogs allowed just 109 total yards, including 10 rushing yards on 32 carries.

3. Miami Hurricanes (1-0, Previous Rank: 4)

Week 1 Result: WIN at Stanford (45-6) Next Week: vs. Florida A&M

The Darian Mensah era in Miami started with a flourish, as the Duke transfer was nearly perfect under center, completing 27-of-30 pass attempts for 401 yards and five touchdowns to kick-start what many expect to be a legitimate Heisman Trophy push.

Last year's freshman standout Malachi Toney also picked up right where he left off, tallying 12 catches for a school-record 234 yards and three touchdowns. Don't be surprised if he is a mainstay in the Heisman conversation himself.

The Hurricanes scored touchdowns on six of their first seven drives, running circles around a Stanford squad that already had a game under its belt with a Week 0 victory against Hawaii. Expect more fireworks next Thursday when Miami squares off against SWAC opponent Florida A&M.

2. Notre Dame Fighting Irish (0-0, Previous Rank: 3)

Week 1 Result: vs. Wisconsin (Sunday) Next Week: vs. Rice

1. Ohio State Buckeyes (1-0, Previous Rank: 2)

Week 1 Result: WIN vs. Ball State (56-3) Next Week: at Texas

The Buckeyes went three-and-out on their first possession of the season, then scored touchdowns on six of their next seven drives to cruise to a lopsided opening victory.

Returning offensive stars Julian Sayin (21-of-25, 320 yards, 3 TD), Bo Jackson (9 carries, 83 yards, 1 TD) and Jeremiah Smith (8 catches, 151 yards, 2 TD) all put up numbers before heading to the sidelines, and 14 different players ended up catching a pass as they finished with 434 yards through the air.

A marquee matchup against the Texas Longhorns in Austin awaits next week, and the outcome will be talked about for the remainder of the 2026 season.

articles.title: Through Chaos and Controversy, Lane Kiffin Proves It's All Worth it for LSU
articles.summary: He is controversial and polarizing. To many, perhaps most, he's bordering on arrogant and profoundly unlikable.
articles.body:
He is controversial and polarizing. To many, perhaps most, he's bordering on arrogant and profoundly unlikable.

He is a master manipulator and an expert at pushing the buttons you don't want pushed. Those sitting on barstools in Oxford, Mississippi would have plenty more to say—things that could never be printed here.

But as the dissections of Lane Kiffin have persisted ever since he boarded his private plane for Baton Rouge—leaving a program smackdab in the middle of a College Football Playoff run—one thing has never been debated.

The man can coach. He can recruit. He can build a program with ample resources.

For all the things that have and will be said about Kiffin—some very rightfully said, for that matter—the results and impact are undeniable.

All of it was on display on Saturday night in Death Valley, where lightning delayed Kiffin's debut but couldn't slow him down.

On paper, LSU and Clemson looked like a fascinating matchup between two teams that couldn't afford a loss. Then the game started.

LSU scored 51 points, Clemson scored 10.

LSU racked up 644 yards of offense, Clemson finished with 145 yards.

The game never actually felt that close.

While an early Sam Leavitt interception created a moment of tension that cascaded throughout Tiger Stadium, that error was soon erased. The LSU offense took control, Leavitt settled in, and Kiffin's new-look offensive and defensive lines took control of the game.

If we're being completely honest, Clemson didn't stand a chance.

For all that flash that comes with Kiffin and the teams he coaches, this was a game of effort and execution. This was a game won in the trenches, and LSU showcased plenty from the very start.

For as much chaos as Kiffin has generated over the past month, LSU's game plan was surgical.

The team was ready. Emotions were in check. Despite the many days spent talking about judges and courtrooms and the moral conundrum of NFL players returning to college football, none of it mattered.

When the game began, it was all business.

A roster that was largely overhauled with the help of many millions of dollars, more than four dozen players becoming a team in a matter of months, gelled together brilliantly. A staff largely made up of former Ole Miss coaches knew the ritual despite the dozens of new faces playing an actual football game together for the first time.

It shouldn't have looked this easy and put together. It shouldn't have looked this dominant. Despite all the money spent on this roster, even the most optimistic LSU couldn't have expected a first game this grand.

At halftime, with the score 31-3, Kiffin seemed disgusted when asked about his team's performance, specifically the first interception. Then, as the interview ended, a familiar character appeared.

"Imagine if we had pro players," he told ESPN's Holly Rowe.

Indeed, the architect of it all has spent the better part of the past few weeks exploring every possible edge to improve his roster further. While LSU ultimately decided not to add NFL players for the time being, Kiffin has become a national talking point and enemy No. 1 in the SEC.

In many respects, it's all part of the Kiffin playbook. Sure, he took a few years off in some respects, remaking his image through social media and a prolonged sense of calm that couldn't last.

This is who he is, for better or worse. It doesn't really matter where you stand on him at this point; it won't change him.

He doesn't just operate in the chaos; he thrives in it.

On Saturday night, we saw a glimpse of what Kiffin's influence and LSU's reach can look like as a marriage. The prospects are intoxicating.

The danger, of course, is looking too deeply at one result. Clemson's roster was depleted by NFL departures, and the current version looks like a middling ACC team at best. LSU's performance is one story to be told; Clemson's anemic showing is another.

At the very least, we must show restraint when evaluating what LSU's dominating win means long term.

Often, football games lie. Even ones like this.

Time will tell exactly what this means, especially with meaningful opponents just a few weeks away, but that shouldn't damper a wildly successful debut and the potential that accompanies it.

Saturday night's result didn't suddenly make Kiffin more likable or less polarizing. Those who wish to see him fail again will have plenty of chances soon enough.

But for a moment, there was calm. No judges or courtrooms or lawyers. No rumors of transfers or NIL wizardry.

Just football. Glorious, well played football.

The only chaos to be found came on the scoreboard, which was remarkably one-sided. It's the kind of chaos Baton Rouge could get used to.

articles.title: Peterborough artist's journey from council estate to Dragons' Den
articles.summary: Nathan Murdoch recalls being doubted by his boss when he walked away from a decade-long career.
articles.body:
"You're leaving here to draw on garage doors?" Nathan Murdoch recalls his former chief executive quizzing him.

It was the summer of 2018 and Murdoch, then in his early 30s, had decided to leave behind a decade-long career as a health and safety manager to pursue life as a full-time artist.

His boss's reaction "made me doubt myself", he says. But eight years later, the 40-year-old from Peterborough has built a successful street art business, painted murals around the world and, last week, appeared on Dragons' Den .

His week since appearing on the BBC One business programme has been "pretty intense".

"I've had messages on social media, I've gained new followers, I've had job offers. The opportunities have been insane."

It was not the first time the dad-of-two had found himself in the spotlight.

His mural of The Prodigy frontman Keith Flint was an online hit in 2020, and other artworks have attracted national media coverage.

He has got used to being recognised in his hometown, but says it has stepped up over the past week.

"I was at a petrol station on the A1 and a guy asked me if I'd been on Dragons' Den. It was surreal," he says.

The growing recognition is a far cry from Murdoch's childhood. He describes himself as a "poor council kid from Peterborough" who was arrested as a teenager for graffitiing the city.

"I say to the young kids now that in the early 2000s graffiti was hated," he says.

"Banksy wasn't popular, street art didn't exist. In 2004, camera phones didn't really exist, the internet didn't exist like it did now.

"My mum told me I had to stop doing it."

After leaving school he worked in factories, "but I needed more, so I worked my way into a health and safety role".

"When I joined that job, I thought it would be the last job I'd ever do," says Murdoch.

"It was for a prestigious British brand that made yachts. It felt like the pinnacle of my life, like I'd achieved something."

He quietly built an art business in his spare time, until one day his director asked to speak with him about his future.

"I actually told him I was thinking of leaving… no-one really knew what I did on the side. When I told him I was thinking of leaving to become a street artist, he just laughed."

Later that day, he says he was offered an £8,000 pay rise, which he accepted. But three months later, he found himself quitting his job for good.

"My gut was telling me I don't want to get to 40 years old and wonder 'what if?'. I thought I wouldn't be able to live with myself.

"It was the scariest thing I'd ever done. I had a mortgage, a child, my wife was on maternity leave. She asked me if I could do it and I said, 'I think so'."

Since then, Murdoch's business has taken him around the world, but he says he still identifies as working class.

"My friend came round the other day and he said I'm so middle class now and burst out laughing because I've got a pizza oven," he says.

"On paper, he's right. I don't think I want to admit it – I think I'd still call myself working class but sometimes I feel guilty saying it. I'm not rich, but I'm miles away from where I started."

Although Murdoch did not secure investment during his appearance on Dragons' Den, he did come home with the offer of a job from entrepreneur Steven Bartlett.

"I am working with his team and him to make it happen," he says. "I'm hoping we'll have it done by the end of the year. There are some designs in progress."

Does he ever see himself going back to the corporate world?

"Sometimes I think it's hard and think maybe I should go back to a day job – business is a challenging thing," he says.

"I thought when the business got bigger life would get easier, but as a famous rapper once said, more money, more problems. But I don't think I could go back to the day job.

"If I decided to give it all up tomorrow, I feel like I achieved more than I ever thought I would do and I'm completely content with that. Anything from now is just a bonus."

articles.title: Dante Moore Says Boise State 'Motivated' Oregon By Dancing During 'Shout' Tradition on Video
articles.summary: The Isley Brothers' timeless 1959 single, "Shout," has been played between the third and fourth quarters of Ducks home games at Autzen Stadium since 2010.
articles.body:
The Isley Brothers' timeless 1959 single , "Shout," has been played between the third and fourth quarters of Ducks home games at Autzen Stadium since 2010.

On Saturday, visiting Boise State decided to dance en masse to the song as the Broncos tried to mount an upset bid against the No. 2 Ducks with the score tied at 24.

Ducks quarterback Dante Moore had some comments on the matter. Of note, the moment apparently fueled Oregon.

"We seen it. We laughed at it," Moore said, per Ira Gorawara of The Athletic. "We went there and put points on the board. It motivated us."

The two teams traded field goals in the fourth quarter, but Oregon ended up winning 34-27 in part because Moore connected with wide receiver Dakorien Moore, who showed some sensational shiftiness and speed for a 62-yard touchdown.

Moore had some other comments on Boise State's dance.

"It was funny that they did the Shout," Moore said, per Gorawara. "It was a little weird."

As Gorawara noted, Oregon did something similar two years ago, when the Ducks danced to House of Pain's "Jump Around" at Camp Randall Stadium, home of the Wisconsin Badgers. The "Jump Around" tradition, which also occurs between the third and fourth quarters, started at Wisconsin in 1998.

Moore was asked if what happened Saturday reminded him of what occurred in 2024.

"I sure did," Moore said, per Gorawara. "Actually, they were just doing something that we've done before, and that's just trying to flip your mind when you find a way to try to steal the juice from the crowd."

Overall, credit goes to Boise State for having fun and staying loose in the moment. The Broncos ultimately fell to Oregon in a hard-fought game but showed why they should be taken very seriously this year.

Meanwhile, Moore showcased why he's considered a Heisman candidate and potential high NFL draft pick by producing on an afternoon where Oregon didn't play its A game.

articles.title: Lane Kiffin Says LSU's Mock Team Scored More Than Clemson After 51-10 Win in Tigers HC Debut
articles.summary: LSU head coach Lane Kiffin reacted to his team's blowout victory over Dabo Swinney and Clemson in their season-opening clash, winning by the final score of 51-10 at Tiger Stadium.
articles.body:
LSU head coach Lane Kiffin reacted to his team's blowout victory over Dabo Swinney and Clemson in their season-opening clash, winning by the final score of 51-10 at Tiger Stadium.

When asked by ESPN's Laura Rutledge about how the contest compared to LSU's mock game ahead of the matchup, Kiffin said that his mock team fared better than Clemson did.

"Our mock team scored more points against us than them," Kiffin said (h/t John Eads of WAFB-TV).

LSU didn't open the game on a high note, as a pass from quarterback Sam Leavitt was intercepted on the team's first possession.

The Tigers got back on track quickly and ended up taking a 17-3 lead at the end of the first quarter, though.

LSU found the end zone twice in the second quarter, holding a 31-3 advantage at halftime before cruising to the victory during the final two quarters.

Kiffin's squad finished with 38 first downs and 644 total yards. This included 309 rush yards, as LSU averaged 5.3 yards per carry as a team.

Leavitt went 16-of-28 for 230 yards and one touchdown compared to one interception. He also rushed for 113 yards on 12 attempts, scoring twice on the ground.

Winston Watkins Jr. was Leavitt's top target, hauling in seven receptions for 110 yards and a touchdown.

Meanwhile, LSU running back Dilin Jones picked up 113 yards and two touchdowns on 23 carries.

The Tigers moved to 1-0 as they begin Kiffin's first year patrolling the sidelines in Baton Rouge.
